report:
## Conclusion

Your view is supported by good but not entirely uniform evidence. The key trial, Tuuli et al. (NEJM 2016), a well-conducted single-center RCT of 1,147 women, found chlorhexidine-alcohol significantly reduced surgical-site infection versus iodine-alcohol (4.0% vs. 7.3%; RR ~0.55) (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048). Several other RCTs and observational studies echo this, including an Indian trial showing 6.95% vs. 14.28% infection rates favoring chlorhexidine (https://www.ijrcog.org/index.php/ijrcog/article/view/6461), and a pilot RCT trending the same direction though not reaching significance (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8369632/).

However, not all trials agree. The larger, pragmatic CAPICA trial found no significant difference in SSI between chlorhexidine-alcohol and povidone-iodine (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28599898/), highlighting heterogeneity possibly due to formulation, application technique, or population differences.

A recent network meta-analysis synthesizing multiple RCTs concluded that chlorhexidine 2% in alcohol was the most probable top-ranked agent for reducing SSI after cesarean, followed by alcohol-based povidone-iodine (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0195670124001282), aligning with broader surgical literature (non-obstetric clean-contaminated surgery) showing chlorhexidine's superiority (pooled OR 0.68) as cited in related meta-analyses.

**Bottom line:** The preponderance of evidence, especially the rigorous NEJM RCT and network meta-analytic ranking, supports chlorhexidine-alcohol as more effective than iodine-alcohol for reducing SSI after cesarean delivery. However, at least one large RCT (CAPICA) found no significant benefit, so the effect, while probably real and clinically meaningful, is not perfectly consistent across all high-quality trials—likely reflecting differences in formulations and technique rather than disproving the overall direction of benefit.
